title: Winter and Smile
premise: Orsen Winterbourne hosts a late-night call-in show, and for two weeks the callers have all been people who died the week before — including, eventually, his own grandmother. When he returns to her house to settle the estate, every photograph has gained an empty chair, and each night another chair fills with a seated figure he cannot quite see. The house is running a count: it keeps residents until their number comes up, then makes them sign papers transferring their name, face, and memories to whatever waits in the chairs. Orsen must get his scattered family out ahead of the count before the last living resident signs, but the final signature on the inheritance documents turns out to be his own, dated decades before his birth.
about_author: Paloma Kavanagh is the pen name of a former overnight radio producer who spent years logging calls from insomniacs, grief-stricken widows, and voices she could never quite place. She writes horror about families that keep things — houses, names, debts — long after they should have let them go.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. During his 2 a.m. show, a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday; Orsen assumes a prank and plays it for laughs on air. The emotional beat is cocky denial — he's built a career on not believing anything his listeners say.

chapters.title: The Second Caller
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The same voice calls again, angrier, reciting details of Orsen's childhood no stranger could know. His producer Maren quietly pulls the call log: the number belongs to a cemetery payphone. Beat: first hairline crack in his skepticism.

chapters.title: Grandma's Voicemail
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A voicemail from Grandma Ida arrives three days after her death, cheerful, mid-sentence, asking him to 'count the chairs before you sign anything.' He listens eleven times. Beat: grief weaponized into dread.

chapters.title: The Estate
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, arriving at the decaying family house in Hollow Creek. His sister Delphine is already there boxing dishes, brittle and hostile. The lawyer, Mr. Voss, is too eager for signatures. Beat: homecoming as trap-springing.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Sorting photographs, she notices every family picture now includes an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before — at weddings, at Christmas, in Ida's graduation photo. Beat: shared delusion begins, or shared sight.

chapters.title: Count the Chairs
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He photographs the walls; by morning one chair has moved closer to the camera in every image. He counts fourteen chairs. The family records list thirteen residents, ever. Beat: arithmetic becomes horror.

chapters.title: Maren's Research
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. At the station archive she finds the show's frequency was once used by a 1930s program called 'The Winterbourne Hour,' hosted by a man whose voice matches Orsen's exactly. Beat: inheritance reaches backward.

chapters.title: Delphine Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Voss pressures her to sign preliminary papers; she refuses on instinct and finds her own name already printed on a page dated next month. Beat: defiance and terror braided together.

chapters.title: Night One in the House
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He stays over against Delphine's advice. At 2 a.m., the radio in Ida's room switches itself on; a caller — Ida — tells him the count is at twelve and dropping. Beat: the dead become allies.

chapters.title: The Family Tree With Roots
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. In the attic he finds a ledger of residents spanning 140 years, each entry closed with a signature and a date of 'transfer.' Every Winterbourne is listed. Beat: the scale of the inheritance revealed.

chapters.title: Cousin Ruthie Arrives
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. A cousin neither sibling has met in twenty years shows up uninvited, warm and wrong, asking pointed questions about who intends to stay. Beat: the house has begun recruiting.

chapters.title: What Ruthie Signed
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Flashback chapter: broke and grieving, Ruthie signed Voss's papers years ago for money; since then her reflection lags half a second behind her. Beat: the price of survival made personal.

chapters.title: Twelve
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A neighbor dies unexpectedly; that night only twelve chairs appear in the photographs, and one holds a shape like heat-shimmer. Beat: the count is real, external, and indifferent.

chapters.title: Maren Comes to Hollow Creek
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. She brings the archive tapes; playing the 1934 broadcast in the house causes every chair to scrape simultaneously toward the parlor. Beat: knowledge is dangerous but necessary.

chapters.title: Voss's Office
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He confronts Voss, who speaks of the estate as an employer, a duty, a mercy — 'someone must always be resident.' Voss's own name appears nowhere in any record. Beat: the antagonist's serene bureaucracy.

chapters.title: Delphine's Bargain
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Terrified for her kids, she secretly offers Voss herself in exchange for their exemption. He says the house doesn't trade down, only up. Beat: maternal sacrifice meets cosmic accounting.

chapters.title: The Voice on Line Two
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Broadcasting remotely from the house, he takes a call from a listener claiming to be Orsen Winterbourne — the original, transferred in 1936, begging him not to sign. Beat: identity as relay race.

chapters.title: Eleven
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven across one night. Another death in town; eleven chairs; Ruthie begins sleepwalking toward the parlor each night, smiling. Beat: the net tightening around the weakest.

chapters.title: The Photographs Move
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. The pictures now show the seated figures faintly — generations of Winterbournes, faces blurred where the house hasn't finished copying someone. One blur is wearing Orsen's face. Beat: recognition horror.

chapters.title: Ida's Instructions
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Through the dead-radio, Ida explains the rules: the count falls until one resident remains; the last one signs for everyone; the chairs take what's signed away. Get out ahead of the count, or be counted in. Beat: rules established, hope kindled.

chapters.title: Running the Count
chapters.summary: Orsen and Delphine's alternating POV. They try to get everyone out of county lines; Ruthie's car dies at the border every time, engine turning over on a voice counting down. Beat: escape attempt and its elegant failure.

chapters.title: Ten
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Ten chairs. Maren realizes her own grandmother's name is in the ledger — she was a Winterbourne before her marriage. She is already resident. Beat: the protagonist circle shrinks.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He finds a room behind Ida's closet wall containing every transferred resident's belongings, perfectly preserved, labeled in careful handwriting — including a suitcase with HIS initials, packed for a trip he's never taken. Beat: fate as luggage.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Last Smile
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie stops resisting. She sits in the parlor at dusk, content, and asks Delphine to remember her 'as the version that got to rest.' By morning nine chairs remain. Beat: surrender as tragedy, not defeat.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Grief and fury; he broadcasts live from the parlor daring the house to take him on air. Callers — dozens of the transferred dead — warn him in chorus: don't sign, don't sit, don't smile back. Beat: defiance as ritual.

chapters.title: Voss's Error
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine tricks Voss into revealing the mechanism: the papers require a willing signature from the last resident, and willingness can be manufactured but not forced. Beat: a rule to exploit.

chapters.title: The Forged Will
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. They attempt to forge transfer papers naming a dead man as last resident. The ink dries into the ledger's handwriting and the house laughs through the radiators. Beat: hubris punished, plan one dead.

chapters.title: Eight
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Eight chairs. Maren chooses to stay and keep broadcasting the warnings, becoming the story's chronicler. Her beat: acceptance without surrender — she'll fight from inside the count.

chapters.title: Childhood, Revisited
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The house floods him with manufactured memories of a brother he never had — softening him, making him lonely enough to want company. Beat: the house attacks through longing, not fear.

chapters.title: Delphine Breaks
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Isolated from her children by Voss's paperwork, she nearly signs. Orsen talks her back from the table using their grandmother's voicemail, played aloud. Beat: siblings finally fighting on the same side.

chapters.title: Seven, Six, Five
chapters.summary: Compressed montage across POVs as deaths accelerate in Hollow Creek — an epidemic no doctor can explain. The town empties; the house grows warmer, brighter, almost welcoming. Beat: dread through acceleration.

chapters.title: The Original's Confession
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The 1936 Orsen Winterbourne gets through on air: he signed willingly, believing he was saving his daughter. The daughter was Ida. The chain was always meant to end with our Orsen. Beat: inheritance revealed as design.

chapters.title: Four
chapters.summary: Orsen, Delphine, Maren, and Voss are the last residents standing. Voss finally sits down at the table, satisfied — he was never staff; he was the house's first signature, waiting to come home. Beat: betrayal inverted into revelation.

chapters.title: Three
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Voss transfers; three chairs left. The house offers Orsen everything — Ida alive in the photographs, the brother restored, the show forever. It is a genuinely good offer. Beat: temptation at maximum sincerity.

chapters.title: The Unwilling Signature
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine realizes willingness can be broken as well as made: a signature given under false pretenses is void. She provokes the house into lying to Orsen on tape. Beat: the loophole armed.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen sits at the table, pen in hand, and asks the house to state its terms truthfully. It lies — it cannot help lying — and Maren broadcasts the lie county-wide. Beat: climax pivot; the pen hovers.

chapters.title: Winter and Smile
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He signs his refusal across the inheritance page, smiling deliberately at the chairs — giving nothing, keeping his name. The house shrieks through every radio band as the count runs backward. Beat: the title's meaning fulfilled.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Dawn. The chairs are gone from the photographs; the ledger's pages blank themselves; Voss's office stands empty and dusty, long abandoned. Maren's grandmother's name fades from the tree. Beat: exhausted, disbelieving relief.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Weeks later, Orsen hosts his final broadcast, thanking listeners who may or may not all be alive. Ida's voice calls once more, just to say goodbye properly. Beat: mourning completed, identity kept.

chapters.title: One Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV, epilogue. At Thanksgiving, the family gathers at Delphine's new house. Everyone sets the table; everyone counts twice. There is one extra chair, and it stays empty on purpose — set for whoever comes next, on their terms. Beat: vigilance as inherited wisdom, survival's ongoing price.
